title: Level 1 – Qualified Nurse
subtitle: Caring for Adults with Confidence
intro: Welcome to GNPS Program 4 - Caring for Adults with Confidence. Adult medical-surgical nursing forms the centre of everyday hospital practice. Nurses care for adults experiencing acute illness, long-term conditions, surgery, pain, reduced mobility and changing physical function. Safe care begins with a structured assessment and a clear understanding of how illness affects the whole person. This level is designed around the adult health capabilities expected within national nursing education programs and by nursing regulatory bodies in different countries. It develops the practical knowledge, clinical reasoning and professional behaviours required to assess adults, plan care, recognise deterioration and deliver safe interventions across hospital, clinic and community settings. Throughout this level you will strengthen your ability to: Complete a systematic assessment of an adult patient Relate common symptoms to underlying pathophysiology Use the nursing process to develop an individualised care plan Recognise priority problems using airway, breathing and circulation Provide safe care for common cardiovascular and respiratory conditions Support adults with renal, gastrointestinal and endocrine conditions Prepare patients for surgery and provide postoperative care Prevent common complications including falls, pressure injuries and infection Educate patients and families about recovery and self-management Adult patients often present with several conditions at the same time. A person admitted with pneumonia may also have diabetes, reduced mobility and kidney impairment. Nurses must connect assessment findings, identify the most urgent need and coordinate care without losing sight of the patient's comfort, dignity and goals. By the end of Level 1, you should be able to assess adults with common medical and surgical conditions, develop safe nursing care plans and respond appropriately to early signs of deterioration within your scope of practice.

content.text: Adult medical-surgical nursing focuses on caring for people who experience acute illness, chronic disease, injury or surgery. The nurse must understand the condition while also considering pain, mobility, nutrition, emotional wellbeing, family support and the person's ability to manage after discharge. Effective care is organised around the nursing process: assessment, diagnosis or problem identification, planning, implementation and evaluation.
Learning outcomes
Explain the scope of adult medical-surgical nursing Describe the stages of the nursing process
Relate pathophysiology to common clinical manifestations Identify factors that influence an adult patient's response to illness

The Adult Patient as a Whole Person A medical diagnosis describes the disease, but nursing care addresses how the disease affects the person. Breathlessness may reduce mobility and sleep; pain may limit coughing after surgery; financial or family concerns may affect recovery. Assessment should include physical, psychological, social, cultural and functional needs.

Pathophysiology and Clinical Presentation Understanding how a condition alters normal body function helps the nurse interpret symptoms and anticipate complications. Heart failure can produce fluid accumulation and breathlessness. Infection may cause fever, confusion and low blood pressure. Diabetes may delay wound healing and increase infection risk.

The Nursing Process Assessment gathers information. Problem identification interprets the findings. Planning establishes priorities and measurable goals. Implementation delivers interventions. Evaluation determines whether the plan is effective and what should change. The process is continuous rather than a single written exercise.

Prioritisation Airway, breathing and circulation provide an immediate framework for urgent problems. Nurses also consider acute versus chronic findings, stable versus unstable patients and expected versus unexpected changes. Safety and life-threatening concerns take priority.

Mr Singh is admitted with pneumonia. He has fever, productive cough, low oxygen saturation and weakness. The nurse first addresses breathing by positioning him upright, applying prescribed oxygen and completing respiratory assessment. The nurse then plans hydration, medication, mobility and education. Care is prioritised according to immediate risk while remaining person-centred.
Key learning points
Treat the person, not only the diagnosis Use pathophysiology to interpret assessment findings
Apply the nursing process continuously Prioritise airway, breathing, circulation and immediate safety

A thorough assessment provides the foundation for every nursing decision. Adult patients may deteriorate gradually, and early clues can be subtle. Clinical reasoning involves collecting cues, comparing them with the patient's baseline, interpreting their meaning and deciding what action is required.
Learning outcomes
Conduct a structured head-to-toe assessment Recognise normal and abnormal findings
Interpret trends in vital signs and basic investigations Use clinical reasoning to identify priority nursing problems

History and Baseline The nurse should establish the presenting problem, medical history, medications, allergies, function, nutrition, elimination, sleep, pain, cognition and social circumstances. Knowing the patient's usual condition makes new changes easier to recognise.

Physical Assessment A systematic assessment includes general appearance, airway, breathing, circulation, neurological status, skin, abdomen, mobility and devices. Findings should be recorded objectively and compared with previous observations.

Vital Signs and Trends A single observation may appear acceptable while a trend shows deterioration. Rising respiratory rate, falling oxygen saturation, new tachycardia, reduced urine output or increasing confusion may be early warning signs.

Diagnostic Information Laboratory and diagnostic results support assessment. Nurses should understand the clinical meaning of common tests such as full blood count, electrolytes, renal function, blood glucose, arterial blood gases, ECG and chest imaging within their scope.

Mrs Chen is recovering from abdominal surgery. Her blood pressure remains within the normal range, but her respiratory rate has risen, urine output has fallen and she appears restless. The nurse recognises that the trend may indicate early deterioration, repeats observations, assesses the wound and fluid balance, and escalates promptly.
Key learning points
Establish the patient's usual baseline Assess systematically rather than relying on one symptom
Look for trends and combinations of abnormal findings Escalate concerns before severe deterioration occurs

sections.title: Nursing Care for Common Medical Conditions

content.text: Adults commonly require nursing care for cardiovascular, respiratory, renal, gastrointestinal and endocrine conditions. The nurse's role includes monitoring, administering treatment, preventing complications, supporting function and teaching the patient how to manage the condition.
Learning outcomes
Describe priority nursing care for common adult medical conditions Monitor response to treatment and identify complications
Apply safe fluid, oxygen, nutrition and medication-related care Support self-management and health promotion

Cardiovascular Conditions Patients with hypertension, coronary artery disease or heart failure require assessment of pain, circulation, fluid balance, activity tolerance and response to medication. New chest pain, severe breathlessness, hypotension or arrhythmia requires urgent review.

Respiratory Conditions Asthma, COPD and pneumonia can reduce oxygenation and increase work of breathing. Nursing care includes positioning, respiratory assessment, oxygen therapy as prescribed, inhaled treatment, hydration, sputum management and recognition of fatigue or respiratory failure.

Renal and Fluid Balance Conditions Acute or chronic kidney impairment may cause fluid overload, electrolyte changes and reduced medication clearance. Accurate intake and output, daily weight, blood pressure, oedema assessment and review of renal results are essential.

Gastrointestinal and Endocrine Conditions Abdominal pain, vomiting, bleeding, altered bowel function and poor nutrition require careful assessment. Diabetes care includes blood glucose monitoring, medication safety, nutrition, foot care and recognition of hypoglycaemia, hyperglycaemia or infection.

Mr Ali has heart failure and diabetes. He becomes more breathless, gains two kilograms in three days and develops ankle swelling. The nurse reviews fluid balance, oxygen saturation, lung sounds and blood glucose, administers prescribed therapy, escalates the change and teaches him why daily weight monitoring is important.
Key learning points
Connect symptoms with the affected body system Monitor both disease progression and treatment effects
Use fluid balance and weight as important clinical indicators Teach patients how to recognise worsening symptoms

Surgical nursing begins before the procedure and continues through recovery and discharge. Nurses prepare patients physically and emotionally, confirm safety requirements, monitor postoperative recovery and prevent complications such as bleeding, infection, respiratory compromise, venous thromboembolism and pressure injury.
Learning outcomes
Prepare an adult patient safely for surgery Perform priority postoperative assessments
Recognise common postoperative complications Promote recovery through pain relief, breathing exercises and mobility

Preoperative Care Preoperative nursing includes confirming identity, consent processes, fasting status, allergies, medication instructions, investigations and preparation requirements. The nurse also explains what the patient can expect and reduces anxiety through clear communication.

Immediate Postoperative Assessment Airway, breathing, circulation, consciousness, pain, wound, drains and urine output are priorities. Observations should be compared with baseline and the type of procedure performed.

Preventing Complications Deep breathing, coughing, early mobilisation, thrombosis prevention, pressure care, aseptic wound care and adequate hydration reduce postoperative risk. Pain should be managed so that the patient can breathe, move and rest effectively.
Recovery and Discharge Patients need clear instructions about wound care, medication, activity, diet, follow-up and warning signs. Discharge planning should begin early and consider support at home.

After knee surgery, Ms Brown reports increasing calf pain and swelling. The nurse recognises possible venous thromboembolism, stops unnecessary mobilisation, assesses the limb, escalates urgently and follows the clinical pathway. Early recognition prevents delay in treatment.
Key learning points
Surgical safety begins before the operation Prioritise airway, breathing and circulation after surgery
Prevent complications through early evidence-based actions Teach clear warning signs before discharge

End-of-Program Summary By completing GNPS Program 4 - Level 1, you have developed the foundational knowledge and clinical skills required to assess adult patients, understand common medical and surgical conditions, plan nursing care and recognise early deterioration. These capabilities prepare you for Level 2 - International Qualified Nurse, where the focus expands to complex care, international standards and multidisciplinary coordination.
